71.title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
71.hook: two sad travelers walk seven miles with a stranger and know him when he breaks bread
71.howItsDone: Many churches read the road to Emmaus in the Easter season, and some hold Emmaus walks on Easter Monday. Christians often speak of meeting Christ in scripture and in the breaking of bread, the two halves of many Sunday services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabboni: Mary Magdalene knew the risen Jesus by her own name. Today a new stretch begins.

After bad news, the walk home goes over it and over it. What happened. What should have happened. What it all means now. The same Sunday, Luke says, two followers of Jesus are walking away from Jerusalem, toward a village called Emmaus, threescore furlongs off, about seven miles. One is Cleopas; the other, Luke never names. They're talking it all over: the arrest, the cross, and a strange report from some women about an empty tomb. And a stranger falls into step beside them.
screen: `THE WALK HOME AFTER BAD NEWS.` → `SEVEN MILES TO EMMAUS.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.`

segments.voice: Luke tells us who it is, in the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him." He asks what they're discussing, and they stop, faces sad. Cleopas says: are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Then this line: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel." We had hoped. Past tense. The stranger doesn't correct them right away. Starting with Moses and all the prophets, he explains the scriptures about the Messiah. At the village he acts as if he's going further, and they stop him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." The hymn Abide with Me borrows that line. At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them: the same four movements as anamnesis, and the feeding on the hillside. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight." They say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" That same hour they walk the whole way back, though the day was far spent, to tell the others how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Luke's story goes on in a second book, the Acts of the Apostles, and this road is the hinge. The story doesn't end at the tomb; it turns around on a road and keeps going.

segments.voice: Find one we had hoped of your own, a plan that fell through, a door that stayed shut, someone who left, and say it the way the two did: I had hoped. Then walk back over the last few days, as they looked back over the road, to a moment that warmed you while it happened, a talk, a meal, a kindness, you only noticed afterward. Rest there; if you pray, give thanks for it.
Emmaus. A village seven miles from Jerusalem, where two sad travelers recognized the stranger who had walked with them, in the breaking of the bread.
Your line: our hearts burned. Tomorrow, the disciple who missed it all. That's seventy-one days.

72.title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
72.hook: the one who wanted proof gets invited to touch the wounds
72.carry: doubt is allowed in the room
72.howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, which Orthodox Christians call Thomas Sunday. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, in India, trace their church to the apostle, and many churches keep his feast in July or December.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emmaus, where hearts burned and the stranger was known in the breaking of bread. Today, someone who wasn't convinced.

You've missed something big. The group chat is exploding. Everybody was there except you, and what they're telling you sounds impossible. Back in Jerusalem, there's a locked room. On the evening of that first Sunday, John says, Jesus came and stood among the disciples, said peace be unto you, and showed them his hands and his side. But one of the twelve wasn't there: Thomas, called Didymus, the twin. When the others tell him, we've seen the Lord, he doesn't just nod along.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE BUT YOU.` → `A LOCKED ROOM, A FIRST SUNDAY.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: Thomas says, in the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's where doubting Thomas comes from. But look at who he was before. When Jesus decided to go back into Judea, where, his disciples reminded him, people had just tried to stone him, Thomas said: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." And at the last supper, when Jesus spoke about going away, Thomas was honest enough to say, we don't know where you're going; how can we know the way? Read that way, he doesn't look like a skeptic by nature. He's brave, and he asks what others may be thinking. Eight days later they're together again behind shut doors, and Thomas is with them. Jesus stands among them: "Peace be unto you." He goes straight to Thomas, offering exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't throw Thomas out for doubting. He comes back for him. And a surprise: the text never says Thomas touched him, only what he answered: "My Lord and my God." Some readers hear it as one of the fullest confessions of who Jesus is in the Gospels, from the one who doubted. Then Jesus says: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." Tradition says Thomas later carried the news as far as India, and the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.

73.title: Breakfast on the beach (John 21:1–19)
73.hook: by a charcoal fire, Jesus asks Peter three times: do you love me?
73.howItsDone: Many Christians read John 21 as the story of Peter's restoration after his denials, and preachers often use it to speak about forgiveness and second chances. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also read 'feed my sheep' as part of Peter's commission to lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas, the twin, who wanted proof, then said: my Lord and my God.

Some things between friends never get mentioned. They just sit there. By the sea of Tiberias, in Galilee, some days after the empty tomb, Peter says he's going fishing, and six of the others go with him. All night, nothing. At dawn a figure on the beach calls: throw the net on the right side of the boat. It fills so heavily they can't haul it in. One of them says, it is the Lord, and Peter pulls on his coat and jumps into the water. On the shore a fire is already burning, with fish on it, and bread: come and have breakfast. But something still sits between Peter and Jesus, and the fire is the kind Peter has seen before.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `IT IS THE LORD.` → `COME AND HAVE BREAKFAST.`

segments.voice: John uses one Greek word for a charcoal fire at two moments. The first is the night of the arrest, in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter warms his hands and says three times that he doesn't know Jesus. The second is this beach: same fire, same smell of smoke. After they eat, Jesus asks, in the King James Bible: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Yes, Lord, you know I love you. Feed my lambs. He asks again. And a third time. Readers can hardly miss the match with three denials. John says Peter was grieved at the third, and he answers like someone with nothing left to prove: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says, "Feed my sheep." Nobody brings up the courtyard. No lecture, no probation. Each yes is answered with a job: look after the people I love. John's Greek uses two verbs for love here, agapao and phileo, and readers argue about whether it matters. Some hear a shift in the kind of love; others think John just varies his words, as elsewhere. The text doesn't settle it. Churches hear the charge differently: Catholics and Orthodox Christians hear feed my sheep as Peter given a shepherd's work in the church, and many Protestants hear it above all as a picture of what grace does for anyone who has failed. What they share is the shape: three denials, three loves, and then a future.

Without pretending it didn't happen, picture handing them something to do again, a little trust back. If you pray, bring their name to God; if not, hold the picture and notice how it sits in you.

74.title: The ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
74.hook: he's lifted out of sight, and two men ask why they're staring at the sky
74.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate Ascension Day on the Thursday forty days after Easter, and Christians confess in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds that Jesus ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a charcoal fire on a beach and three questions: three denials, three loves.

A car pulls away. A hand waves from the back window until the corner; the street empties, and the person on the sidewalk keeps looking anyway. The Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. Acts says that after the empty tomb Jesus appeared to his friends for forty days. Gathered with him one last time, they ask what they've carried all along: is this the moment you restore the kingdom to Israel? He says the timing isn't theirs to know. Then, as they watch, he's lifted up, and a cloud takes him out of their sight. And they stand there, staring at the sky.
screen: `WAVING FROM THE BACK WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before he goes, Jesus gives them the map of the whole book of Acts: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." Jerusalem first, then Judea's countryside, then Samaria, the neighbors with an old quarrel, then everywhere. Then he's gone, they're still looking up, and two men in white stand beside them. In the King James Bible: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" It's almost funny: the sky has just opened, and heaven's first words are, why are you still standing here? The men promise he'll come back the same way, and the disciples walk back down to Jerusalem, to wait and pray. Luke tells this scene twice, at the end of his Gospel and at the start of Acts. Nothing in the text suggests a trip into outer space. In the Bible a cloud is an old sign of God's presence, from the cloud over Sinai to the bright cloud on the mountain of light, and the churches' old creeds say that he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father: Jesus taken fully into God's presence, not gone for good. Christians differ on how literally to picture the rising, and the text doesn't say how it looked. Many churches keep Ascension Day forty days after Easter, on a Thursday, though some move it to the Sunday after. But the heart of the story is the question. Stop staring. Go.

The ascension. Jesus taken up out of sight, forty days after Easter, and his friends sent back down the hill.

75.title: Pentecost (Acts 2:1–13)
75.hook: wind, flames, and every visitor hears the good news in their own language
75.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit and the birthday of the church. Many churches decorate in red, read Acts 2, and sometimes read it aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ascension, and two men in white: stop staring at the sky; go.

A street market in a big city on a holiday weekend: every stall shouting, a grandmother bargaining in one language, a kid answering in another. That's Jerusalem on the morning of this story. It's a Jewish festival, and pilgrims have come from all over the known world. Acts lists them: Parthians and Medes, people from Mesopotamia, Egypt and Libya, Cretes, Arabians and visitors from Rome. Meanwhile about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus wait together in one house, as they were told to. Then, Acts says, a noise from the sky like a violent wind fills the whole house. A crowd comes running, and what they hear next makes no sense at all.
screen: `A CITY OF LANGUAGES.` → `ONE HOUSE, WAITING.` → `A SOUND LIKE WIND.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Flames, resting on each person. And they begin to speak in other languages. The crowd hears Galileans, country people from up north, speaking their own mother tongues: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Some are amazed. Some sneer that they're full of new wine. Peter stands up: they're not drunk, it's nine in the morning. Pentecost is Greek for the fiftieth day. Jews had long counted fifty days from Passover to the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, a harvest festival that many Jews also came to link with the giving of the law at Sinai. The miracle: nobody is made to speak one language; everyone hears in their own. The good news doesn't ask the crowd to cross over to it; it crosses over to them. Many Christians read this as the undoing of Babel, the old story where one language was scattered into many. Here the many languages stay, and understanding comes anyway. Christians call Pentecost the birthday of the church, understand it as the coming of the Holy Spirit, and keep it fifty days after Easter, often in red, the color of flame. Pentecostal churches take their name from this day, and many pray in tongues; other churches see the gift as belonging mainly to the early church, or as rare. All of them keep the picture: every language.

segments.voice: Picture someone you'll see this week whose language isn't yours, a first language or a grandparent's slang, a teenager's, a coworker's jargon, and ask how they'd say hello. 76.title: They shared everything (Acts 2:37–47)
76.hook: the first community breaks bread in homes and shares what they own
76.tomorrow: the beggar at the Beautiful Gate
76.howItsDone: Many churches hold up Acts 2:42 as a pattern for church life: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Monastic communities and some Protestant communities hold property in common; many other Christians practice it through giving and shared meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost: wind, flame, and a crowd from everywhere hearing their own mother tongues. Every language.

A shared house has a group chat, and the group chat has opinions. Whose turn is it. Who ate the last of the bread. Sharing sounds lovely until it's Tuesday. Back at Pentecost, the same day, Peter has just finished speaking, and Acts says the crowd were cut to the heart and asked: what shall we do? He tells them to turn around and be baptized, and about three thousand people do, in a single day. Many are visitors far from home, and the small group from Galilee has no buildings, no budget and no plan. What happens next, Luke tells in one short paragraph.
screen: `WHAT SHALL WE DO?` → `THREE THOUSAND IN A DAY.` → `NO BUILDING, NO PLAN.`

segments.voice: Luke gives four things they kept doing: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer. The word for fellowship is koinonia, from koinos, common, shared: having a share in something together. Luke shows what that looked like: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and gave to anyone as they had need. They met in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes, and here's the source of our line: they "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Meat, in the King James Bible's English, just means food. Singleness of heart: a heart that isn't divided. Glad and simple hearts. Now the honest part. Acts doesn't pretend it stayed easy. A few chapters later a couple lie about what they gave, and there's an argument about widows being left out of the daily food. Christians have read it in different ways ever since. Monks and nuns took it as a pattern and hold everything in common to this day, as do some Protestant communities like the Hutterites. Many other Christians read it as a picture of radical generosity, given freely, rather than a rule for every church. Whichever way you read it, nobody is told to share. They just do. And the bread keeps turning up: in homes, around tables, day after day.

segments.voice: Let your mind walk through where you live, room by room: the shelf, the closet, the kitchen. 77.title: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10)
77.hook: Peter has no money, so he gives what he has: the man walks, leaps, praises
77.carry: such as I have, give I thee
77.howItsDone: Christians often quote Peter's words 'silver and gold have I none' when speaking about giving time, attention and care, and some churches' Sunday readings come from Acts 3 in the weeks after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, koinonia: a shared life, bread broken in homes, and glad and simple hearts.

You're coming out of a store and someone by the door asks for change. You pat your pockets. Nothing. Who carries cash these days? So you do the little shrug, the half smile, and keep walking, not quite looking at them. Now the temple in Jerusalem, three in the afternoon, the hour of prayer. Peter and John are walking up. At the gate called Beautiful, a man lies on the ground, unable to walk since birth. Every day someone carries him here, so he can ask the people going in to pray for a coin. He sees Peter and John and asks. And Peter has no money either.
screen: `NO CASH. THE SHRUG.` → `THE GATE CALLED BEAUTIFUL.` → `CARRIED THERE EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: First, Peter stops. He fixes his eyes on the man and says: look at us. Before anything else, the man is seen. He looks up, expecting a coin. And Peter says, in the King James Bible: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk." He takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and his feet and ankles grow strong. Luke doesn't let him just stand there: "And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God." Walking and leaping: the man carried to the door every day goes in through it on his own feet. Peter doesn't pretend to have what he hasn't got, and he doesn't feel bad about the empty pockets and walk on. He gives what he actually has. In the name of Jesus, for Christians, means by his authority and power, not Peter's: the story is careful that Peter isn't the healer. And the people who see it know this man; they've walked past him for years. Where exactly was the Beautiful Gate? Nobody knows for certain: it's named nowhere else in the Bible, and scholars still debate which of the temple's gates it was. But the line has lasted: such as I have, give I thee.
screen: `LOOK ON US: FIRST, HE'S SEEN.` · `SILVER AND GOLD HAVE I NONE.` · `WALKING, AND LEAPING, AND PRAISING.` · `GIVE WHAT YOU ACTUALLY HAVE.` · then, large: `SUCH AS I HAVE GIVE I THEE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, honestly, what you have today: maybe not money, maybe not energy, but perhaps ten minutes, a skill, a kind word, a good ear, the ability to look someone in the eye and say, I see you. Pick one, and one person who could use it. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, just hold it ready.
